title: why Catholics say "presence"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter: the women walking in the dark, and the empty tomb. Your line was: the stone is already moved. Did you take one step? Day seventeen.

Watch Catholics walk into an empty church on a Tuesday afternoon. No Mass, no music, nobody at the front. And yet, before they slide into a pew, many of them drop to one knee, facing a small box of gold or wood near the altar, with the little red lamp burning beside it. You met that lamp on day nine. Why kneel to a box in an empty room? Because Catholics don't think the room is empty. On day five we saw the bread and wine at Mass, and promised to come back to the big claim. Today we do. Why Catholics say presence.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHURCH ON A TUESDAY.` → `ONE KNEE, FACING A SMALL BOX.` → `NOT AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: The word is Eucharist, from the Greek eucharistia, which means thanksgiving. At the Last Supper, the Gospels say, Jesus took bread and gave thanks. So the whole meal is named after a thank-you. Here's the claim. Catholics believe that when the priest says the words of the Last Supper at Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. They still look, taste and feel like bread and wine. But what they are, underneath, has changed. The Church calls this transubstantiation, a word it formally used starting in the Middle Ages, and it calls the result the real presence. Not a symbol of him. Him. Catholics point to John's Gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." And then even more bluntly: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." John says many followers found this too hard and walked away. Jesus didn't soften it. He let them go. That's the backbone of Catholic belief here. And after Mass, the consecrated bread that's left over is kept in that small box, the tabernacle. That's why the red lamp burns, and why people kneel as they come in. They believe he's there. Christians understand this differently, and it's worth saying plainly. Orthodox Christians also believe in a real presence, usually without using that Latin word. Lutherans speak of a real presence too, in their own terms. Many other Protestants understand communion as a memorial and a sign. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, Jesus promises: "I am with you all days." Catholics hear the tabernacle as that promise, kept in a room. He stayed.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `STILL LOOKS LIKE BREAD.` · `I AM THE LIVING BREAD.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE LAMP.` · then, large: `HE STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of a time someone simply stayed with you. They didn't fix anything. They sat in the hospital waiting room, or on the end of your bed, or on the phone while you cried. Remember what it felt like not to be alone. Let that feeling fill the whole time. If you pray, you can rest in the thought that you're not alone now, either. The bell holds the time.
The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the bread and wine Catholics believe become Christ's body and blood, his real presence. Seventeenth word.
Your line: he stayed. Today, stay with someone a little longer than you need to: on the phone, at the table, at the door. Day seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering a church, and many spend quiet time in prayer before it, a practice called adoration.
